notes:
THE ROW THAT CLOSES THE LAST ESCAPE HATCH, and it closes one I opened a few hours earlier.

Row 24 found that a photographed blue callout arrived at delta_s 0.016, and I wrote that IF a photographed blue or green highlighter lost saturation the same way, saturation could not find it at all. It does not. A real cyan marker photographed holds its colour: four marks at delta_s 0.125-0.137, hue 172-175, on cream paper whose own hue is 48. The 86% loss row 24 measured belongs to photographing a GLOWING SCREEN through room light, not to cool colours under a camera. That inference was too broad and this row corrects it.

BUT IT ALSO BREAKS THE THING ROW 24 LEFT STANDING. Row 24 argued that the camera path had not inverted -- refuse at 0.153, find at 0.196, a window 0.043 wide. In a common colour space the camera rows now read:

    0.129  row 25, cyan marker            FIND
    0.153  row 24, yellow callout         REFUSE
    0.196  row 10, pink on cream          FIND

A real mark sits BELOW a thing that must be refused. The camera path is inverted too, and 'saturation is the wrong primary test' is no longer a statement about screenshots. It is both sources.

THE WITHIN-PAGE SPREAD IS THE OTHER HALF, AND IT IS SMALL. Four marks, one pen, one page, one exposure: delta_s 0.125 to 0.137, a spread of 0.012. The pink series spans 0.32 across rows. So nearly all the variance that defeats a threshold comes from the PAGE and the PATH, not from the stroke. A per-page normalisation is right and already in F1; what it cannot do is make one page's numbers comparable to another's.

PAPER S IS 0.157 ON THIS PAGE, which is higher than row 24's entire yellow callout delta (0.153). Aged cream paper is more saturated than some things a detector has to refuse. The record already had an aged page at paper S 0.153 making the case against an absolute threshold; this is a second, and on this page the paper's saturation very nearly equals the marks' margin above it.

HUE WOULD WORK BEAUTIFULLY HERE AND THAT PROVES NOTHING. Paper 48 degrees, marks 172-175: about 125 degrees apart, near the maximum possible separation. Row 3 is the other half of the lesson -- warm paper at 43-50 against yellow marks at 50-53, a collision. Hue separates a COOL mark from WARM paper and fails when both are warm. Still naming, not finding.

THE FILL RULE GETS ITS FIRST COOL MARKER. V drop 0.059-0.086, far under max_v_drop 0.45, and in the same band as every other real mark (0.00-0.35). The earlier cyan-on-a-form measurement sat at 0.35, the top of that band, so cyan spans 0.06-0.35 depending on the page. The rule holds; its margin is page-dependent.
